findings.quote: diagnostic manuals also require the incongruence to have been present for months rather than briefly, and to cause significant distress or difficulty in daily life
findings.explanation: The sentence follows a description of ICD-11 and then says 'diagnostic manuals' (plural) require months of duration and significant distress. That is the DSM-5-TR gender dysphoria criterion (at least six months; clinically significant distress or impairment). ICD-11 gender incongruence (HA60/HA61) does not make distress a requirement, and WHO moved it to the chapter on conditions related to sexual health, out of the mental disorders chapter, as this page's own overview says. As written, a reader is told ICD-11 also needs distress, which contradicts the page's definition ('The mismatch itself is called gender incongruence and is not an illness'). The same blurring appears in the title and aliases, which treat 'gender dysphoria' (the distress) and 'gender incongruence' (the mismatch) as one thing.
findings.suggestedFix: Attribute each manual separately, for example: 'DSM-5-TR (gender dysphoria) requires incongruence for at least six months with clinically significant distress or impairment; ICD-11 (gender incongruence) does not require distress.' Or delete the sentence. Consider removing 'gender incongruence' from the aliases, or state that the page covers both terms.

findings.quote: Urgent care for very high glucose readings with drowsiness or confusion, a foot wound that is red, hot or discharging, sudden vision change, or chest pain.
findings.explanation: Chest pain should point to 999/A&E (possible heart attack, which can be atypical or painless in diabetes), and drowsiness or confusion with very high glucose suggests hyperosmolar or ketoacidotic crisis, an emergency. The type-1-diabetes page uses 'Emergency care' for drowsiness or confusion in diabetes, so the two pages give different urgency for the same feature. 'Urgent care' reads as an urgent GP appointment. The same loose tier is used for chest pain in conditions/chronic-kidney-disease seekCare ('Urgent care for breathlessness, chest pain, severe drowsiness...'). The field also never tells a reader with the classic new symptoms (thirst, passing urine often, weight loss) to see a GP, and the symptoms list omits them.
findings.suggestedFix: Split into tiers: 'Call 999 or go to A&E for chest pain, or drowsiness or confusion with very high glucose readings; same-day GP or NHS 111 for a red, hot or discharging foot wound or sudden vision change; see a GP for increased thirst, passing urine more often or weight loss.' Apply the same wording to the chronic-kidney-disease page.

findings.quote: The first step is a short period of rest with simple pain relief, followed by physiotherapy; most people treated this way recover and return to normal activity.
findings.explanation: Contradicts the opening sentence of the same field ('Stay active, pain relief ..., physiotherapy, and time'). Current UK guidance (NICE NG59 on low back pain and sciatica; NHS) advises staying active and keeping to normal activities as far as comfort allows, not resting; rest is associated with slower recovery. 'The first step is a short period of rest' is therefore both internally inconsistent and out of line with UK advice.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite to match the first sentence, for example: 'The first step is to stay active within comfort, with simple pain relief, followed by physiotherapy if symptoms persist'; remove 'a short period of rest'.

findings.quote: foot
findings.explanation: The anterior cruciate ligament is an intra-articular ligament of the knee. The page lists the foot skeleton as the affected organ, while the site has a 'knee' organ (Knee joint, organs.json) that is not listed. Readers and the knowledge graph will link an ACL tear to the foot.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace 'foot' with 'knee' in affects.organs (the femur, tibia and patella structures are already correct).

findings.quote: When osteoporosis comes from another condition or a medicine, treating that cause comes first, for example by lowering the dose or switching the drug responsible.
findings.explanation: Reads as advice to reduce or change the medicine responsible. Glucocorticoids and other long-term medicines must not be reduced or stopped without the prescriber (abrupt steroid withdrawal can cause adrenal crisis or relapse of the underlying disease). UK practice (NOGG, NICE) is to assess fracture risk and start bone protection alongside necessary glucocorticoid treatment, not to defer it until the cause is dealt with. The prevention field has the same instruction-style phrasing ('review medicines that cause falls or bone loss').
findings.suggestedFix: Describe rather than instruct: 'When osteoporosis is secondary to another condition or a medicine, the prescriber reviews the cause and whether the medicine is still needed, and bone-protective treatment is often started at the same time. Medicines should not be stopped or reduced without medical advice.'

findings.quote: Emergency care for vomiting, abdominal pain, deep breathing, drowsiness or confusion in someone with diabetes, or for severe hypoglycaemia (confusion, seizure, unconsciousness).
findings.explanation: The field covers emergencies in people already known to have diabetes only. It never tells someone with the classic new-onset symptoms described in the overview (thirst, passing urine often, tiredness, weight loss), above all a child or young person, to seek same-day assessment, although a substantial minority of children are first diagnosed in ketoacidosis. NHS advice is to see a GP for these symptoms and to call 999 for signs of ketoacidosis, and NICE NG18 asks for same-day referral of children and young people with suspected type 1 diabetes.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a sentence such as: 'See a GP urgently, the same day for a child or young person, for increased thirst, passing urine more often, tiredness and weight loss: these can be the first signs of type 1 diabetes.'

findings.quote: None yet, although immunotherapy can delay onset in high-risk relatives; good control prevents complications.
findings.explanation: 'Good control prevents complications' is a promise. Intensive glucose control lowers and delays the risk of retinopathy, nephropathy and neuropathy (DCCT/EDIC) but does not prevent them, and complications occur in people with excellent control; the wording can also read as blame.
findings.suggestedFix: Change to 'good control lowers the risk of complications'.

findings.quote: Screening is directed at older women and at younger women with additional risk factors.
findings.explanation: There is no UK population screening programme for osteoporosis. NICE CG146 and the National Osteoporosis Guideline Group advise opportunistic fracture-risk assessment (FRAX or QFracture) in women aged 65 and over, men aged 75 and over, and younger people with risk factors (check the current NICE version). The sentence reflects US screening policy, omits men, and is not attributed to a country on a UK-first site.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace with the UK position (no national screening; case-finding by fracture-risk assessment per NICE CG146 and NOGG), or label the sentence as US practice.

findings.quote: and for blood in the urine, pain on passing urine with fever, or sudden confusion in an older person, which may indicate infection.
findings.explanation: Visible blood in the urine is grouped with signs of infection. Haematuria needs prompt assessment because it can be due to bladder or kidney cancer or stones as well as infection (NICE NG12 refers unexplained visible haematuria in adults aged 45 and over on the suspected-cancer pathway). The page's own diagnosis paragraph lists blood in the urine as a reason for cystoscopy and specialist referral.
findings.suggestedFix: Separate it: 'Blood in the urine needs prompt assessment by a GP, because it can come from infection, stones or cancer.'

findings.quote: Urgent care for palpitations with breathlessness or chest pain, fever with confusion and agitation, or sudden vision change or eye pain.
findings.explanation: Fever with confusion and agitation in someone with an overactive thyroid is the picture of thyroid storm, which the page itself calls rare and life-threatening, and palpitations with chest pain or breathlessness can mean a dangerous rhythm or cardiac ischaemia. These need 999/A&E, but they sit in the same 'urgent care' tier as sudden vision change or eye pain, while the type-1-diabetes and hypothyroidism pages reserve 'Emergency care' for comparable features.
findings.suggestedFix: Use two tiers: 'Call 999 or go to A&E for chest pain, severe breathlessness, or fever with confusion or agitation; same-day assessment for sudden vision change or eye pain.'

findings.quote: Autoimmunity against citrullinated proteins, in genetically susceptible people, often triggered by smoking or infection
findings.explanation: States a cause as fact. Anti-citrullinated protein antibodies are present in only about 60 to 70 percent of people with RA (seronegative RA is common), so this is not the mechanism of RA in general. Smoking is an established risk factor, especially for antibody-positive disease, but infectious triggers (periodontal bacteria, viruses) are hypotheses, not established causes. The cause of RA is not known.
findings.suggestedFix: Soften to: 'The cause is not fully understood: an abnormal immune response (often with anti-citrullinated protein antibodies) in genetically susceptible people; smoking is the best-established environmental risk factor.' Remove 'or infection'.

findings.quote: Pituitary gland
findings.explanation: The 'affects' block lists breasts, testes, ovaries, uterus, prostate, pituitary gland and hypothalamus as organs and structures affected by the condition. Gender incongruence is not a disease of these organs (the page says it is not an illness and that no single biological cause is established); they are the targets of hormone therapy and surgery. Listing the pituitary and hypothalamus implies a neuroendocrine cause, contradicting the page's own causes field, and presenting the gonads and genitals as 'affected' is neither accurate nor neutral.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove the 'affects' block for this page, or relabel it as 'relevant to care' and drop the pituitary and hypothalamus.

findings.quote: Type 1 or type 2 diabetes
findings.explanation: Autoimmune thyroid disease clusters with type 1 diabetes, and as I recall the cited NIDDK page names type 1 diabetes (not type 2) among the conditions that raise risk; I could not re-check it without web access. Type 2 diabetes is not an established risk factor for hyperthyroidism.
findings.suggestedFix: Change to 'Type 1 diabetes'.

findings.quote: started early, disease-modifying drugs now prevent most damage.
findings.explanation: Overstated prognosis. Early treat-to-target DMARD therapy slows or halts joint damage in many people, but the same page says a 'substantial minority' respond poorly, that DMARDs carry considerable side effects, and elsewhere that they 'slow' destruction. 'Prevent most damage' (and 'early treatment prevents damage' in the prevention field) promises more than the evidence or the page's own text.
findings.suggestedFix: Change to 'started early, disease-modifying drugs slow or limit joint damage in many people'.

findings.quote: PCOS cannot be prevented, but its complications largely can.
findings.explanation: 'Largely can' promises more than is known. Weight management, activity, monitoring and endometrial protection lower the risk of type 2 diabetes, endometrial hyperplasia and cardiovascular disease, but risk stays raised in PCOS, including at a healthy weight, and the cited references do not say complications are largely preventable.
findings.suggestedFix: Change to 'but many of its complications can be reduced by ...'.

findings.quote: Diet and exercise programmes halve the risk in people with prediabetes
findings.explanation: A specific effect size presented as general. Trials (the US Diabetes Prevention Program and Finnish study) reported relative reductions of about 58 percent over a few years, whereas routine programmes such as the NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme report smaller effects, and benefit wanes. Neither cited reference (NHS: Type 2 diabetes; WHO: Diabetes) gives this figure.
findings.suggestedFix: Say 'Structured diet and activity programmes reduce the risk of prediabetes progressing to type 2 diabetes' and cite a source if a figure is kept.

findings.quote: The 'sepsis six' within an hour: oxygen, blood cultures, intravenous antibiotics, intravenous fluids, lactate measurement and urine output monitoring
findings.explanation: The only references are NHS: Sepsis and WHO: Sepsis, which are public-facing and do not set out the 'sepsis six' bundle, NEWS/qSOFA scoring, or the overview's 'each hour of delay in antibiotics raises mortality'. The UK sources for these are NICE NG51, the UK Sepsis Trust and the Academy of Medical Royal Colleges. The page also gives 'over 22/min' for fast breathing, which matches neither qSOFA (22 or more) nor the NICE NG51 high-risk respiratory rate (25 or more).
findings.suggestedFix: Add NICE NG51 and UK Sepsis Trust as references, or soften to 'hospital teams use time-critical bundles of tests and treatment'. Align the respiratory-rate threshold with the named score.

findings.quote: Emergency care for colicky pain with fever or shivering, vomiting preventing fluids, pain not controlled by painkillers, or a single functioning kidney. NHS advice is to ask for an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111 for severe pain or for fever and chills.
findings.explanation: Two different urgency levels are given for the same feature in one field: 'Emergency care' for colicky pain with fever or shivering, then an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for 'fever and chills'. Fever with a stone suggests an infected, obstructed kidney, which the page's overview and complications call an emergency, so a reader could follow the lower tier.
findings.suggestedFix: State one tier: 999/A&E (same-day emergency assessment) for fever or shivering with stone pain; NHS 111 or an urgent GP appointment for severe pain without those features.

findings.quote: Neuromuscular training programmes (landing technique, hip and hamstring strength, balance) cut injury rates by half in athletes.
findings.explanation: A specific effect size for all athletes, stated as fact. Meta-analyses of neuromuscular training report roughly halved risk, mostly in female athletes with good adherence, and results vary. None of the page's references (MedlinePlus knee injuries and ACL, NHS Scotland ACL guidance, PMC8730351 on conservative versus surgical treatment) covers prevention.
findings.suggestedFix: Say 'can substantially reduce injury rates, particularly in female athletes who follow them regularly' and cite a prevention source, or remove the figure.

findings.quote: older adults may have no urinary symptoms and instead show confusion resembling dementia, marked fatigue or incontinence
findings.explanation: Presents confusion, fatigue and incontinence without urinary symptoms as a UTI presentation. UK guidance (NICE NG109, UKHSA UTI diagnostic tool) cautions that bacteriuria is common in older adults and that non-specific features such as confusion, falls or fatigue should not on their own be attributed to UTI (other causes, including sepsis and medicines, need looking for), and that urine dipsticks are not recommended for diagnosis at 65 and over. The diagnosis field recommends a dipstick without that caveat. I am less sure of this one because patient-facing NHS pages do list behaviour change as a possible sign.
findings.suggestedFix: Add the caveat that UTI should not be assumed from non-specific features alone in older adults, and that dipsticks are unreliable at 65 and over.

notes: No high-severity problems found: the slice is generally accurate and UK-first, and the inclusive wording (trans men, non-binary people, trans women) in breast cancer, cervical cancer, ectopic pregnancy, endometriosis, fibroids, ovarian cancer, prolapse, PCOS and urinary incontinence is accurate, respectful and matches the cited UK Government screening guidance. I had about 25 candidates and kept the 20 that matter most; the rest are below. (1) Pattern: 'Urgent care' is used loosely for 999-level features on type-2-diabetes, chronic-kidney-disease ('Urgent care for breathlessness, chest pain, severe drowsiness, or a sudden fall in urine output') and hyperthyroidism; other pages use 'Emergency care' for the top tier. A site-wide convention (999/A&E versus same-day GP/NHS 111) would help. (2) Minor internal tensions not reported: hypothyroidism definition says the immune system is 'most often' the cause while the overview says iodine deficiency is the commonest cause worldwide (true only in iodine-sufficient countries such as the UK); chronic-kidney-disease aliases 'kidney failure' and 'renal failure' conflict with 'a minority reach kidney failure' and can be read as acute kidney injury; disc-herniation lists 'sciatica' as an alias although the overview says sciatica is not a diagnosis in itself (probably deliberate for search); osteoporosis overview calls hip fractures 'largely preventable', which is optimistic. (3) UK-first nuances at low confidence: disc-herniation treatment (muscle relaxants, short courses of stronger analgesia) reflects MedlinePlus, whereas NICE NG59 advises against routinely offering opioids and against benzodiazepines, gabapentinoids and oral steroids for sciatica; hypothyroidism diagnosis cites only US bodies on screening, and its prevention field lists 'screening in pregnancy', which is not routine UK practice; type-2-diabetes risk factors say 'Hispanic' and 'over 40' (NICE risk tools start at 25 for South Asian and Black groups); kidney-stones says alpha blockers and calcium-channel blockers 'can aid passage', whereas the UK SUSPEND trial found no benefit, so the wording should be hedged (I could not confirm what NICE NG118 currently says); hyperthyroidism lists carbimazole and propylthiouracil as equal options (UK practice: carbimazole first line) and never mentions the agranulocytosis warning (sore throat or fever needs an urgent blood count). (4) Time-sensitive: gender-dysphoria says puberty blockers in England are available only through research pathways; this needs re-checking against the current NHS England position. (5) Link and taxonomy observations: the medications lists on sepsis (amoxicillin only) and urinary-tract-infection (amoxicillin, not the nitrofurantoin or trimethoprim named in the text) use the only antibiotic pages that exist, so a reader may take amoxicillin as the usual treatment; osteoporosis imaging omits the existing dxa-scan page; hypothyroidism 'affects' lists pituitary and hypothalamus but not the thyroid (no thyroid organ exists); type-2-diabetes symptoms omit thirst, frequent urination and weight loss; urinary-incontinence symptoms list only abdominal-pain. The hormone-tests links on gout, osteoporosis and rheumatoid arthritis are intentional (that page covers uric acid and vitamin D by site convention). (6) Quotes were checked against content/conditions.json; paths are the JSON field paths.
